summary:
The magnetic effect of electric current is an important phenomenon that has many practical applications in our daily lives.

When two magnets are brought close to each other, their unlike poles (North-South) attract each other. This attraction occurs because like poles repel each other and opposite poles attract each other. In the context of electromagnets, this attraction is due to the magnetic field produced by the current flowing through the coil.

The polarity of an electromagnet can be determined by observing how it behaves when a compass needle is placed near it. If the north pole of the compass is attracted towards one end of the coil (A), then that end is the south pole. This is because like poles repel each other, and in this case, the north pole of the magnet is repelled by the south pole of the compass.

The strength of the magnetic field produced by an electromagnet depends on several factors, including the number of turns of the coil and the current flowing through it. A single cell provides a small amount of current, resulting in a weak magnetic field that can only attract a few clips. However, adding more cells to the battery increases the current, making the magnetic field stronger and allowing the electromagnet to attract more clips.

The number of turns of the coil also affects the strength of the magnetic field. A coil with more turns produces a stronger magnetic field than one with fewer turns. This is because each turn of the coil adds to the overall magnetic field produced by the current flowing through it. Additionally, the increase in the number of turns makes the electromagnet a stronger magnet.

The magnetic effect of electric current has many practical applications, such as in devices like electromagnets, electric bells, motors, fans, loudspeakers, and more. These devices rely on the magnetic field produced by the current flowing through the coil to function.

The magnetic effect of electric current also has important implications in our daily lives. For example, it is used in many household appliances, such as refrigerators and air conditioners, which rely on magnetic fields to operate.
